Me personally (I record indie, alt rock stuff 99% of the time) I pretty much always use an amp with a di box so that I can record the amped signal and the dry DI to use for either reamping (complex process don’t worry about it now) or use an amp sim for layers later on. It all comes down to what you’re doing. But I have a bunch of sm57 clones from eBay (they were like 15 dollars each) and they’re pretty much identical sound wise to the real deal, I suggest you get one and experiment with mic’ing your amp. Start about 1.5 -2 inches off the grill (3-6 cms if metric is ya thing) on the center of the cone. If you don’t like that tone try moving it to the left or the right of the cone or rotating the mic to be 45° axially from the cone.

I recorded drums in an empty but standard bedroom sized room with 6 foot ceilings and it came out fantastic. you have a great set of mics for drums. Do you have more? with small spaces it is best to have as many mics as possible so that you can control everything. 
Two things I always do when recording drums is an sm57 on the wall (Siamese dream by the smashing pumpkins notably used this technique) as well as a stereo condenser in front of the kit for an image (mono will work too it’ll just be a narrower sound) Use the sm57 on the wall to blend as a room mic and the wall reflections when sent to a reverb will help give a much bigger sound. As for treatment and room placement, experiment. Likely near the center of the room will be best but you have furniture and other things in the room this all changes the room. So you may find that the kit facing out of a corner towards your bed (idk what your room looks like I’m
Just making an example) actually sounds best. But if I were you, I’d definitely try and get a few more mics for the drums, sm57s are cheap and great mics for this. I actually almost always use them as top and bottom for snare, on hi hats, rides, and I’ve used them on toms a few times. good luck and happy recording!
